newsitem.title: USA: U.S. steady rates show Fed awaits slowdown-experts.
newsitem.headline: U.S. steady rates show Fed awaits slowdown-experts.

text.p: The Federal Reserve's decision to leave short-term interest rates alone indicates the central bank is betting -- as it did in 1996 -- on an economic slowdown later this year, experts said on Tuesday.

"The Fed's policy of the last few years has clearly been responsible for the relatively low and steady inflation we have seen," Stephen Cecchetti, professor of economics at Ohio State University, told Reuters.
Cecchetti, an expert on inflation and monetary policy, is to become New York Fed Director of Research this summer.

The Federal Open Market Committee ended a regular meeting with no announcement, leaving the federal funds rate unchanged at 5.50 percent -- its level since a 25-basis-point hike on March 25 for the first credit tightening in more than two years.
The Fed Board has not moved on the 5.0-percent discount rate since January 31, 1996.

Wall Street analysts were almost evenly divided over the outcome of the FOMC meeting, with economists weighing the unusual mix of the economy -- a combination of strong growth, low unemployment and steady inflation at low levels.

"The goal right now for the Fed is to keep the economy on a steady growth path without allowing for increases in inflation," Cecchetti said. "That's the goal. And the right goal is to keep inflation low, which is a pro-growth policy."

Cecchetti noted the underlying inflation trend has remained stable around 3.0 percent while the United States enjoyed a period of solid growth. Cecchetti attributed the steady inflation performance to the preemptive anti-inflation policy the Fed conducted between February 1994 and February 1995.
Earlier this month, sources close to the Fed had told Reuters a preemptive May rate hike was being considered.
The main argument in favor of back-to-back rate hikes was that this would help slow down consumer demand and thus address the risks of inflationary pressures.
But American Express Director Emily Porter said a small 25-point rate hike would have had a negligible impact on consumers using credit cards.

"If your credit card carries an interest rate of 18 percent, and rates go up by 0.25 percentage point, that would not make much of a difference," Porter said. "On a balance of $1,000, you would pay $15 a month in interest and this (rate hike) would mean a little more than 20 cents a month."
SBC Warburg chief economist Ken Bercuson saw the absence of a rate hike as a sign the Fed is betting on a slowdown.

"The absence of a move today shows that the Fed expects the economy to decelerate very quickly over a very short period of time. Unfortunately, in my view, the fundamentals do not support such a conclusion," Bercuson said.

"While demand would slow, it would not slow enough to alleviate pressure on resources. Consequently. I expect inflation to rise over the course of the year," added Bercuson, who noted the expected slowdown of 1996 resulted in robust growth in the fourth quarter and the first quarter of 1997.
Former Fed vice chairman Alan Blinder noted the absence of a rate hike seemed to indicate the Fed is not pursuing an aggressive anti-inflation policy.
"I don't believe that what the Fed is doing now is trying to drive the inflation rate lower as quickly as they can," said Blinder, now a professor of economics at Princeton University.

"It's clear that there are some inflationary risks right now. Different analysts have different evaluations of how large that risk is," Blinder added. "The apparent view of the majority of the FOMC is that the risk is not terribly large and they can afford to wait for more information," Blinder added.
The FOMC next meets in early July. Analysts on Wall Street are already divided about the outlook for that meeting.
